items.title: Dar, Saudi and Turkish FMs follow up on understandings reached in first Makkah Defence Alliance meeting: FO
items.description: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar held phone calls with Saudi Arabian and Turkish foreign ministers on Sunday and followed up on the understandings reached at the inaugural meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance last month, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The joint defence pact was signed on August 7 and empowers the member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Its inaugural meeting was held on August 31 in Istanbul, where it was decided that the alliance’s secretariat would be initially headed by Pakistan for three years. The three countries also agreed to work towards strengthening their defence capabilities and the cohesion of their armed forces through joint activities, robust defence industry cooperation, and joint technology development and production. Moreover, through the institutionalised and resolute implementation of the Makkah agreement, the three countries also agreed to provide essential contributions to regional peace and stability. In a series of posts on social media platform X, FO said that DPM Dar held separate phone calls with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal Bin Farhan and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Sunday. In the call with the Saudi FM, the two leaders discussed regional and international developments, including matters of mutual interest at multilateral fora. “They also discussed follow-up on the understandings reached at the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee of the Makkah Defence Alliance, held in Istanbul, and agreed to remain in close contact,” FO said. In a separate post, FO said that Dar also spoke to Fidan and thanked him for hosting the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Istanbul. FO said the two leaders followed up on understandings reached and discussed ways to further advance cooperation under the framework. “The two foreign ministers also exchanged views on regional and international developments. They also discussed matters of mutual interest and opportunities to further strengthen cooperation at multilateral fora,” FO added. The tripartite agreement was signed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during a summit at Al-Safa Palace. Pakistan has said that the pact is “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. And while Turkiye has said that there is a possibility of Egypt joining the pact, there has been no confirmation from Cairo. Abdelatty invites Dar Earlier in the day, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty invited DPM Dar to visit his country, FO said. A statement issued by the FO said that the two held a telephone call in which they exchanged views on Egypt-Pakistan bilateral relations and regional and international developments. Abdelatty invited Dar to “hold a bilateral visit to Egypt at his earliest convenience”, it added. They also reaffirmed their commitment to remaining “engaged and involved” on regional security matters, agreeing to meet on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) this month. Last November, the Egyptian foreign minister undertook an official two-day visit to Pakistan at DPM Dar’s invitation. During the visit, he met Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, where the two discussed “defence and security cooperation, military exchanges, training collaborations and regional peace and stability”, FO said at the time. Abdelatty also met President Asif Ali Zardari during the visit. Pakistan and Egypt are also members of a quadrilateral regional alliance known as the R-4 Group (Regional Four), an arrangement which also includes Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. The R-4 group has been focused on regional security and emerged in March amid mediation efforts between the US and Iran.

items.title: Abrantie College wins Best Catering School of the Year at Ghana Cake Business Awards 2026

The awards are associated with The Baking Industry Ghana, an organisation focused on promoting, developing and reshaping the baking industry while creating opportunities for growth and advancement among professionals and businesses in the sector. For Abrantie College, the recognition further highlights its growing contribution to skills development in catering and hospitality. Through practical training, experienced industry facilitators and hands-on learning, the College continues to prepare students for employment, entrepreneurship and opportunities across the wider creative and hospitality industries. The institution expressed its appreciation to the organisers of the Ghana Cake Business Awards for the recognition, as well as its students, staff, facilitators and partners for their continued dedication and contribution to the College’s growth and success.

items.title: Kumawu MP calls for urgent action on SHS infrastructure deficits
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Kumawu, Ernest Yaw Anim, has appealed to the government and the Ministry of Education to urgently address infrastructure deficits confronting schools across the country. He said inadequate classrooms, congestion and insufficient accommodation facilities continued to affect teaching and learning in some senior high schools. Mr Anim made the call while supporting 500 BECE candidates in the Sekyere Kumawu District with essential items to prepare them for senior high school. He noted that some students were confronted with inadequate sleeping facilities, including situations where available beds were insufficient to accommodate all students. He therefore called for increased investment in educational infrastructure to provide students with safe and conducive environments for learning. The MP also appealed to the government, the Ministry of Education and the Ghana Education Service to strengthen measures to motivate teachers and improve their working conditions. He said motivated teachers were essential to delivering quality education and preparing students to become responsible and productive citizens. Mr Anim further condemned sexual relationships between teachers and students, describing such conduct as unacceptable. He called on teachers to desist from all forms of sexual misconduct involving students and urged the Ghana Education Service and the Ministry of Education to strengthen monitoring and supervision in schools. He said headteachers, supervisors and other education authorities must ensure that teachers entrusted with the care of children acted professionally and protected the welfare and future of students. Mr Anim said investing in human capital remained one of his major priorities, explaining that the ultimate goal was to see young people from the constituency become professionals who would contribute to the development of the district and Ghana. He expressed the hope that beneficiaries of his educational support would eventually become doctors, nurses, engineers, lawyers, teachers and other professionals. The MP said producing educated, productive and financially independent young people would constitute one of the greatest legacies of his service to the constituency.

items.title: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years
items.description: No matter how you read it, The Power Broker is a serious undertaking. The paperback weighs as much as a brick; to avoid lugging around all 1,344 pages, people have cut it apart at the spine and chunked it into sections. Others have organized in-person Power Broker marathon readings that run continuously for three full days. I decided to try something else. Over the past several weeks, I’ve spent 10 hours paging through Robert Caro’s masterpiece on an e-reader the size of a credit card. It’s magnetic, and small enough to attach to the back of my iPhone without adding any real bulk to my pocket. (Yes, this does mean that I have a screen on the back of another screen.) It’s called the Xteink X3, and at a glance, it looks like a cheap gimmick: more electronic junk made by unknown brands and sold on Temu and TikTok Shop—the kind of thing influencers are always hawking. (Can I interest you in a programmable LED hat for $11.60? Or how about $20 AirPod look-alikes made by “Fhumsh”?) In a sense, it is that. Xteink sounds less like a real brand name than the kind of garbled text you’ll find in AI-slop memes. (Speaking of which, the official website of the China-based company is full of AI-generated photos of people posing with the device.) And indeed, since the X3’s release on Amazon in May, TikTokers and YouTubers have raved about how the device is a steal and you should buy it right now—just click the link in bio. [ From our August 2026 issue: The end of reading is here ] And so I did. On Amazon, the X3 is $69 and tops the “hot new releases” list for e-readers, beating out a slew of Kindles. In person, the Xteink is many things: plasticky. Flawed. Finicky. Nevertheless, it is the single best piece of technology that I have purchased in years. In the two months before getting this cartoonishly tiny e-reader, I finished only one book. In one month with the X3, I read three books without even really trying—and my iPhone’s average daily screen time dipped by 25 minutes. The X3 is great because of its size, not in spite of it. (For once, “fun-size” actually lives up to the billing.) Because this is such a runt of a device, you can stick it to your phone and have an e-reader in your pocket at all times. As a result, I’ve found myself reading on my morning commute, in line at a museum, even while waiting through Netflix ads. The display on my Xteink may be roughly half the size of the smallest Kindle, but the text is big enough to easily read. Even after three straight hours of inching through The Power Broker , my eyes weren’t strained. The device’s size actually helped me develop a different relationship to reading altogether: Because each “page” on the Xteink amounts to just a paragraph or two—and sometimes less—I’m compelled to finish it. And now that I’m onto the next page, I might as well finish that one too. A YouTuber who recently reviewed the Xteink had the same experience—she referred to the uniquely addictive experience of using the device as the “TikTokification of reading.” I know how terrifying that sounds, but consider the outcome: Whenever there’s even a couple of minutes of free time, I now have a healthy alternative to doomscrolling on Instagram. I don’t even have to put my phone down. Flip over the Bad Screen and fire up the Good Screen. For all of its charm, the Xteink is a pretty basic piece of hardware. For $70, you get what you pay for. Other popular e-readers now come with AI-powered recaps, high-definition displays, and Android operating systems. Meanwhile, the Xteink has no touch screen, color display, or backlight for reading in the dark. (Xteink recently launched the X4 Pro, a slightly larger and more expensive model that has a reading light and a touch screen.) Just reading a book on the device isn’t necessarily seamless: The preloaded software is horrific and can’t even display book covers or properly format some text. Unlike with a Kindle, you can’t port over books from Amazon with one click. In spite of itself, the Xteink X3, in all of its 3.7 inches of glory, has become a viral hit. Online, people have posted photos of their Xteink on trips to the Austrian mountains or the Aegean Sea; one anesthesiologist says he tucks it into his scrubs. People are mounting the Xteink X3 to their kitchen hood to display recipes and are making all sorts of bespoke accessories, including 3-D-printed reading lights and a case that looks like a gun ( I’m serious ). Fans have built their own open-source firmware, Crosspoint, that considerably upgrades the device. The version I downloaded displays reading stats and an array of fonts, and it lets me screenshot pages as I read. Late last month, Crosspoint added the ability to access books on Libby, the popular library ebook app. The best thing about the Xteink is not any one feature. It’s that this tiny e-reader is fun in a way so few gadgets are anymore. Despite all our advances, the consumer-electronics landscape of 2026 is predictable and banal. Our laptops, smartphones, and tablets are thinner and more powerful than ever, but that feels like a weak substitute for innovation. Next week, Apple is poised to launch one of its most hyped products in years: a folding iPhone. But even folding smartphones are old news; Samsung released its version in 2019. After shelling out hundreds or thousands of dollars for a new gadget, you might still have to pay for subscriptions and endure annoying ads . Sometimes, your purchases aren’t even really yours. Amazon recently removed the ability to download ebooks you already own and transfer them to non-Kindle devices. In other words, we need more gadgets like the Xteink: cheap, simple, and customizable. With few exceptions, these products are now coming out of China. Neck fans from brands such as JisuLife and Civpower have become sensations for helping people endure the summer heat. Anker’s portable projectors and earbuds are both Wirecutter -recommended. Silicon Valley has left a gaping hole in the gadgets markets, and Americans are more than willing to look elsewhere.

items.title: What’s the Matter With Moderation?
items.description: O ne simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right. And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter. Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. Full of himself even by senatorial standards (one Republican Senate colleague described him to me as a “know-it-all”), Marshall is leery of public forums where he might hear from protesters and tends to speak before thinking—a hazard of his appetite for cable-TV appearances. In nearly six years as a constituent of the senator, I have traveled from one end of Kansas to the other, and I have concluded that passionate supporters of Roger Marshall are the electoral equivalent of jackalopes: If they exist, I have never found one. Should Hamilton break the Senate’s longest GOP win streak, he would score more than an enormous off-year upset; his influence on 2028—a free-for-all to define post–Donald Trump politics—could be even larger. Because Hamilton seeks to vindicate the belief, beleaguered in today’s culture, that moderation is a good thing, not just as an electoral strategy, but as an approach to life. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Texans will decide if Jesus was a lefty ] In Texas, James Talarico’s Christianity seems, at times, to dovetail with uncanny precision with the agenda of secular progressivism. Hamilton’s rhetoric suggests that his Democratic revival tent would be roomier, but at the same time he has so far faced relatively little pressure to translate his disposition into details. He is motivated by “compassion, a belief in safety nets for vulnerable people,” he told me, and also by “fiscal responsibility, limited government, and strong defense.” Such inoffensive straddling may be out of step with today’s politics. “People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad,” El-Sayed explained to Michelle Goldberg of The New York Times . A roiling left has risen to match Trump’s raging right. To win, Hamilton must not only persuade independents and Republicans to vote for him—he must also motivate angry progressives in this time of throat-cutting. If El-Sayed and others like him are the furious faces of the Democratic future, perhaps Hamilton is a DINO. When I asked him if Democrats should seek to impeach Trump a third time, he ventured his belief that “the impeachments in the first term did not accomplish anything”—a claim that dismisses the expression of righteous anger as a political imperative in itself. Hamilton likes to talk about the good that he could accomplish in partnership with the well-liked Senator Jerry Moran, the senior Republican from Kansas. But maybe that’s not what the people, who truly are pissing mad, really want. E mporia is the seat of Lyon County , which in 2024 gave 56 percent of its votes to Donald Trump and 41 percent to Kamala Harris. Yet Hamilton was not in hostile territory when he visited one late-August morning. Gravel City Roasters is a combination coffee shop and art gallery located directly across Emporia’s main drag from the county Democratic headquarters. There is a Pride flag on the wall with Refugees welcome superimposed on its rainbow stripes. The chai, served in mismatched mugs, is excellent. But the comfort zone is narrow here for a 21st-century Democrat. The little city with its college campus is surrounded by farmland that has historically bred beasts, grains, and discontent. In its heyday—the era of William McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt—Emporia was home to the journalist William Allen White, whose Gazette newspaper was a sort of proto-Substack. Readers around the world vibed to his grumbling, which often had to do with the eternal sense of Kansas as undervalued and overlooked. “Go east and you hear them laugh at Kansas; go west and they sneer at her; go south and they cuss her; go north and they have forgotten her,” White wrote in his career-launching screed, dated 1896 and titled “What’s the Matter With Kansas?” Thirteen decades later, an Emporia pharmacist, John Schmidt, picked up the theme, telling me at the coffee shop of the town’s beef processing plant (closed), its Michelin rubber-track factory (downsized), its maker of plastic ice scrapers (victim of a bankrupt holding company), and the nearby drugstore (battered by low reimbursements). The area’s future, too, feels festooned with pink slips. A few dozen people awaited Hamilton, who arrived in a blue blazer and an open-collared white shirt. He immediately went to work shaking hands and nodding thoughtfully. After watching Hamilton campaign half a dozen or so times, the best description I can manage is “pastoral.” Fair enough, I suppose, for a 62-year-old pastor. Hamilton has a soft voice, and his gaze is gentle, intent, and framed by horn-rimmed glasses. His head moves constantly in tiny yeses and no’s, like a seismograph needle registering each quick conversation. After working his way to the rear of the shop—pausing to autograph a woman’s copy of his book on the Holy Spirit—Hamilton used a wireless microphone to tell a joke about hypocritical politicians pretending to know the Lord’s Prayer. “I am a Democrat who actually knows the Lord’s Prayer,” he said. “When it says, ‘give us this day our daily bread,’ it’s reminding us to make sure that people have enough to eat.” USA Today Network / Reuters A sturdy little stump speech rolled out from there, befitting a man who has been crafting sermons since Seinfeld was new. He said he is a fifth-generation Kansan who married his sweetheart a week after high-school graduation and wants to give his granddaughter “a better country.” He said he built a church from nothing to 24,000 members. He said he prayed a year and a half ago that Trump would govern “with wisdom, grace, and compassion,” but found himself watching something quite different. Somebody’s got to do something became Maybe I should do something . Rather than take on Trump directly, however, he aimed the balance of his fire at Marshall, who, Hamilton noted, “has voted for nearly everything the president has done.” Hamilton said he is against tariffs because they hurt farmers, against the Iran war because it drives up fuel prices, against Medicaid reductions because they threaten rural hospitals, and against cuts to food aid because more than 14,000 Kansas children need that support. “Since when did it become woke to care about your neighbor?” he asked rhetorically, aware that his audience was already seeing attack ads trying to tie him to left-wing ideas, and that Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas used an X post to denounce one of Hamilton’s sermons as “heretical.” Don Duncan was part of that audience, having driven to town from nearby Chase County to have a look at the candidate. In the primary, a local Democrat, Christy Davis, drew 113 votes in Chase County, leaving Hamilton with eight; on the Republican side, Marshall got 479. Duncan, a self-described “Democrat who leans independent,” told me he did not think things are as bleak for Hamilton as that would suggest. “It’s just a matter of people getting to know him,” said the retired school administrator and coach. “We need someone to get us back together.” Could that be Marshall? I asked. “I can’t say we ever talk about him,” Duncan answered. A bout 100 miles north and east , amid the big houses and busy shops of Kansas City’s southern suburbs, stands Hamilton’s monument to open minds, the “church for thinking people” that he founded in 1990. The main sanctuary of Leawood’s United Methodist Church of the Resurrection is visible from all directions, an elliptical edifice clad in glass and stainless steel, vaguely reminiscent of Disney’s Space Mountain. Rising 100 feet above a 77-acre campus of auxiliary buildings and parking lots, it features the largest fused-stained-glass window in the world, a work roughly the size of a basketball court. Nine satellite churches in greater Kansas City—four in Kansas; five in Missouri—carry the COR brand to sites around the area and beyond. If the words megachurch pastor conjure images of hellfire oratory and $400 haircuts, Hamilton comes as a surprise, as mild as Jake from State Farm. Yet his success stands in contrast to the decline of mainstream Christianity in his lifetime. Born in 1964 and raised by divorced parents in Prairie Village, one of those same southern suburbs, Hamilton came of age in a time of Protestant crisis. Perplexed by the social upheaval of the 1960s, Hamilton’s United Methodist denomination lost more than 10 percent of its membership in the 1970s and a further 5 percent in the 1980s. What energy there was in American Christianity came from conservative movements energized by opposition to abortion, homosexuality, scientific modernism, and a grab bag of philosophical attitudes derided by evangelicals as “secular humanism.” Even as a teen, Hamilton found this alienating. Drawn to church for its social possibilities—“I didn’t believe in God, but I believed in girls,” he likes to say—the God he eventually embraced was one who delighted in discovery and gloried in progress. God gave us a brain for a reason , he thought, taking to heart the biblical admonition to worship with all of one’s “heart and soul and mind .” In college at Oral Roberts University in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Hamilton “grew more and more interested in the parts of the Gospel that evangelical churches were leaving behind,” he told me during a July interview at a barbecue joint across the state line in Kansas City, Missouri. “I began focusing on scriptures dealing with social justice, ‘rolling down like waters,’ as Amos has it; the caring for widows and orphans; the story of the Good Samaritan. And I noticed that our churches were great at helping the people who came to church, but not so much with the people who were outside.” Trained as a pastor at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Hamilton returned with his young family to Kansas City in the late Reagan years. He soon persuaded his regional bishop to let him start a new congregation for people turned off by what Christianity had become. Though United Methodism suffered a further 29 percent drop in membership from 1990 to 2020, Hamilton’s congregation grew from fewer than a dozen people meeting in a funeral-home chapel to the largest mainline Protestant congregation in America. He credits an idea known to theologians as the via media, the “middle way,” which has roots in ancient philosophy and scholastic Christianity, but had its flowering in Elizabethan England. At its core the idea involves a belief that truth is not to be found on the extremes and that compromise in pursuit of worthy aims is a virtue. Society as Hamilton envisions it is a sort of Newton’s cradle, the toy that is composed of a line of metal balls suspended by threads. When the ball on one end is lifted and released, it swings into contact with the pack, where its energy is conducted to the ball on the other extreme, which swings away in reaction. Energy might come from extremism, but stability lies with the center. [ Peter Wehner: American Christians face a choice ] COR is that stable center, Hamilton maintains, “roughly equal parts Democrat, Republican, and independent,” where inevitable conflicts among freethinking people can be respected and accommodated in pursuit of shared missions. “I am wired to see both sides,” he told me, “which is not the same as saying that all issues are 50–50. I believe cutting Medicaid and closing rural hospitals is just wrong. Making it harder for public schools to serve special-needs students is wrong, and I am willing to talk with anyone to explain why I think so. But I don’t expect everyone to agree with me all the time.” Hamilton hasn’t shied from hard issues as a pastor. When a faction of American Methodists joined forces with culturally conservative congregations in Africa to try to pass anti-LGBTQ ordinances for the denomination, he led the opposition. Criticizing what he saw as a misguided focus on a few biblical verses over a larger Gospel of inclusion and acceptance, Hamilton ultimately concluded that a schism was inevitable, and he was instrumental in negotiating the many details of separation. The thing to notice about that story, as Hamilton tries to turn from pastor to lawmaker, is that the via media was the road not taken by Hamilton and the Methodists when the chips were down. There was no middle ground, and now there are two denominations where there used to be one. Hamilton would likely run into an even more challenging divide in Washington, where the two factions cannot go their separate ways. Can moderation really be an agenda? In the biblical story of King Solomon, when confronted with a seemingly unresolvable impasse, the wise solution was not to split the baby, but for one combatant to surrender for the greater good. That’s not the Washington way. E lectoral politics is, in some ways, just second-grade math: addition and subtraction. Candidates seek to add votes in Column A while subtracting votes from Column B. All of the money, overt or dark; all of the advertisements; all of the pandering and polarizing; all of the door-knocking, the text messages, the awkward TikToks, the yard signs, the stilted visits by candidates to factories, diners, fairgrounds, living rooms, nursing homes, colleges—it’s all about addition and subtraction. For Hamilton, the problem pencils out at around 80,000 votes. Any combination of addition and subtraction that hits this target, whether raising the Democratic vote share or reducing Marshall’s compared with his 2020 victory, will get the job done. That’s a big number in a state the size of Kansas, where about 1.3 million people voted in 2024, but so is the number of people who cram the pews of Hamilton’s sanctuaries each Christmas and Easter: around 100,000 per holiday. As shown by the August 4 results, his stronghold is in Johnson County, home to his church and to about a quarter of the state’s voters. Once a bastion of chamber-of-commerce Republicanism, the county turned purple during its explosive growth in the Baby Boom years and has, in the Trump era, become a relatively safe base for Democratic Representative Sharice Davids. Driving up turnout in Johnson County and other metro centers—working-class Wyandotte County (Kansas City, Kansas), liberal Douglas County (Lawrence, home to the University of Kansas), booming Sedgwick County (Wichita, still the state’s largest city)—will be the keys to Hamilton’s addition problem. As for subtraction, meet Marshall. A retired ob-gyn who calls himself “Doc”—a nickname that hasn’t caught on with Kansas voters—he has distinguished himself as one of Trump’s most obsequious acolytes, though not always the most on-message. Marshall’s ready-fire-aim approach to public speaking has left his candidacy riddled with self-inflicted wounds. Asked whether he’s okay with Iran having ballistic missiles (the program Trump was promising to destroy), Marshall said, “I would prefer they didn’t. But I don’t think that’s the key issue here. I think that they have to be able to defend themselves.” Of rising gas prices triggered by the war: “Freedom is not free. Americans are going to have to make some sacrifices.” When Kansans died on a plane that collided with an Army helicopter over Washington, Marshall blithely blamed their deaths on DEI, a theory unsupported by crash investigators. Having sold his house in central Kansas shortly after being elected to the Senate, Marshall is dogged by allegations that his status as a Kansas resident is largely fictitious. He lists as his residence a roughly 1,200-square-foot cabin on a family ranch property, but for several years his congressionally paid travel plans included frequent stops at his “vacation” home in Florida, which he says has been uninhabitable since suffering severe hurricane damage in 2024. Marshall’s campaign did not respond to my requests to discuss the race for this article, but in a recent social-media post he wrote, “Over the last six years, I’ve averaged 185 days per year in D.C. doing the work you sent me to do, 130 days per year in Kansas with over 300 stops per year across the state, about 35 days of official travel, and 20 holiday/personal days.” When he does visit Kansas, Marshall has avoided open meetings with the public ever since a crowd in a rural community jeered him in March 2025 during Elon Musk’s DOGE fiasco. “The town halls just became non-productive and dangerous,” Marshall told a newspaper in Hays, Kansas. The odor of weakness around the incumbent helped inspire the GOP-dominated legislature this year to spitball easing Marshall out of office in favor of an appointed successor whose term they would extend through 2028. Voilà! No election needed. The scheme died amid criticism that the Constitution doesn’t allow states to change the length of a Senate term, no matter how lame their senator might be. With no choice but to defend Marshall, the GOP is probing for Hamilton’s vulnerabilities. A Massachusetts-based super PAC spent a reported $600,000 on a TV ad that pieces together phrases from sermons to portray Hamilton as “mega-woke.” “Black Lives Matter,” Hamilton says in the ad, “marching for righteousness.” In another moment, marked with an ellipsis on-screen, he says, “By virtue of being white … I have to repent.” The Kansas City Star dug up the June 2020 sermon from which the clip is taken and found Hamilton saying “I have certain benefits by virtue of being educated, white, and male, right?” adding, almost a minute later, “Before I can do anything to help anyone else, I have to have a conversion. I have to repent.” Ted Cruz’s X post avowing that Hamilton held “heretical” views relied on a sermon in which Hamilton says that non-Christians might enter heaven. Marshall thanked Cruz in his own post and added, “Wait until you hear about the ‘hundreds of mistakes in the Bible’ my opponent claims to have found.” In response, the Hamilton campaign shared a quote from Joshua Leu, a pastor of a church in Great Bend, Kansas, where Marshall once served on the board. HuffPost had asked Leu about Hamilton. “I would say that he’s a middle-of-the-road pastor who is willing to listen to all sides, and then based on his understanding of the gospel, try to make the best decision,” Leu said. Attacking Hamilton as a fellow traveler of the progressive left, a democratic socialist in gossamer disguise, might work in Kansas. But there are reasons why even Kansans who reject that portrait as grossly inaccurate might still say no to his candidacy. The party of Lincoln still has deep resonance in a state where people were battling years before Fort Sumter. Bob Dole’s success at amassing power in Washington and using it to funnel money to the state taught lessons in the value of seniority that are still remembered. Western Kansas is not only overwhelmingly Republican, but it is also suspicious of what it regards as the citified East, where Hamilton is from. And not even all of his Johnson County congregation’s members are Hamilton supporters, by the candidate’s own assessment. As the church has grown, some members have griped that Hamilton has become less accessible—an issue that his Senate campaign is likely to exacerbate, to say nothing of actually serving in the Senate. He’s taken a leave from sermonizing for now, but would stay on as senior pastor and preach at least a dozen times a year if elected. A Kansas Democrat starts out in such a deep hole in a Senate race that Hamilton considered running as an independent, but the recent example of the failed independent Greg Orman (who lost a race for Senate in 2014 and governor in 2018) convinced the pastor and his advisers that only a Democrat could unseat Marshall. When voters ask, as they frequently do, how Hamilton would deal with pressure from party leaders, he told me his answer is: “I won’t work for Chuck Schumer; I’ll work for the people of Kansas.” But other candidates in the region—Dan Osborn in Nebraska, Brian Bengs in South Dakota—have chosen the middlest of ways by running as independents. Perhaps Hamilton’s decision to step off the via media by allying himself with one of our nation’s two political parties is a concession to the reality of politics. Before Hamilton can be as nettlesome for Schumer as, say, West Virginia’s Joe Manchin was during the administration of Joe Biden, he first must win in November. Well-intentioned concessions, however, are the beginning of another, much more famous, road. With money continuing to pour in from more than 16,000 donors, Hamilton can answer the attacks. And he has another shield in his armory. A prolific author of books on scripture, prayer, and Seeing Gray in a World of Black and White , Hamilton has created texts and instructional videos that are staples at Bible studies and Sunday-school classes in at least 500 Kansas churches, he told me. This makes him something of a known commodity in rural communities that might otherwise be leery of a big-city candidate. As he calculates, 500 churches averaging 50 people each represents a small army of 25,000 people at least partly inoculated against anti-Hamilton attack ads. He doesn’t expect to win them all in counties where Democrats sometimes number in single digits, and he doesn’t need to. Maybe a handful in each precinct, in the secrecy of the voting booth, stung by the price of tractor fuel and fertilizer, will mark his name, or simply skip Marshall’s. H amilton is not a dynamic political performer ; he doesn’t suck the oxygen from the room. The son of a service-station manager, a husband and father by the end of his teens, Hamilton instead relies on approachability, on his feeling for life as ordinary people live it: sometimes messy; sometimes painful. He seems to genuinely believe that what people have in common matters more than their differences. You can build a church on that. But can you build a campaign? [ Molly Worthen: What the fastest-growing Christian group reveals about America ] Jim Hightower, the former Texas agriculture commissioner turned liberal pundit, used to say, “There is nothing in the middle of the road but yellow stripes and dead armadillos.” But Kansas has—or had—something of a tradition of moderate Republican senators in the not-so-distant past. Nancy Kassebaum, the daughter of former Governor Alf Landon, the Republican Party’s 1936 presidential nominee (even Kansas went for Franklin D. Roosevelt that year), died last month. She served three terms in the Senate, from 1978 to 1997. She was a Republican who worked on health care, voted to ban assault weapons, and opposed, for nearly all of her career, a constitutional amendment to balance the budget. “We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution,” she said. Hamilton might anger partisans on the left and right—in his pews and beyond—by adhering to the middle way. He will need to make compromises in order to win, or, should he win, in order to govern. Politics inevitably sullies religion. But Jesus, in the Gospel of Matthew, also recommends the narrow road instead of the wide and easy one. As a student of the via media, Hamilton surely knows what came for Queen Elizabeth’s moderate vision. The elegant span she championed connecting Catholic structures and rituals to Protestant individualism proved a bridge to nowhere. The decades after her death belonged to the extremists. Rivers of blood flowed across Europe as Catholics and Protestants waged their Thirty Years’ War. In England, sectarian Puritans staged a regicidal revolution. Refugees from religious violence poured into the Americas. Some eras in history are like that, obstreperous and irreconcilable. Hamilton likes to point out that Kansas contains the geographical center of the lower 48 states, and he hopes to find America’s political midpoint too. The risk is that, like so much of the Farm Belt, the center has been hollowed out.

items.title: Conakry : l’UCEG et RMC Cinéma officialisent un partenariat pour renforcer la sensibilisation citoyenne
items.description: La Plateforme nationale de l’Union citoyenne pour l’émergence de la Guinée (UCEG) et RMC (Rouguiatou Mohamed Conté) ont officialisé, vendredi 4 septembre 2026, un accord de partenariat destiné à renforcer leur collaboration autour de la sensibilisation citoyenne, de la promotion de la paix et de la cohésion sociale en Guinée. Officialisée à la Maison des jeunes de Kipé, cette convention entend notamment mettre le cinéma au service de la transmission des messages de sensibilisation auprès des populations, particulièrement des jeunes. Prenant la parole à cette occasion, le représentant de la Plateforme nationale UCEG a expliqué que cette collaboration s’inscrit dans la volonté de l’organisation de contribuer à une nouvelle dynamique au sein de la société civile guinéenne. « Nous sommes une organisation aujourd’hui qui accompagne non seulement les associations et ONG, mais nous voulons faire quelque chose d’historique pour notre pays, la Guinée », a-t-il déclaré. Il a également salué le choix porté par RMC sur l’UCEG, estimant que ce rapprochement repose sur la convergence des objectifs des deux structures. « Si RMC nous a choisis d’abord par rapport à la sincérité de nos actions, cela nous va droit au cœur. Et nous aussi, si nous avons voulu vraiment signer avec RMC Cinéma, c’est compte tenu de l’objectif de l’Union Citoyenne pour l’Émergence de la Guinée », a-t-il ajouté. Pour l’UCEG, ce partenariat constitue surtout un moyen de renforcer les actions d’éducation civique et citoyenne, dans un contexte marqué par la nécessité de consolider la paix et de lutter contre les discours de haine. « Notre pays est confronté à beaucoup de difficultés : des difficultés d’abord d’éducation citoyenne et civique, mais aussi de la promotion de la paix dans notre pays pour lutter contre la haine. Parce que la première richesse de notre pays, c’est notre diversité culturelle », a-t-il souligné. L’organisation entend ainsi s’appuyer sur le potentiel du cinéma et sur la créativité des jeunes qui évoluent dans ce secteur pour toucher davantage de citoyens. « Notre population a besoin de conscientisation. À partir du moment où nous avons une vision pour créer une nouvelle jeunesse, nous pensons que notre message peut beaucoup passer à travers le cinéma », a-t-il conclu. De son côté, Mohamed Rouguiatou Camara, coordinateur de la troupe RMC Cinéma 224, a insisté sur la portée de cette collaboration, qu’il présente comme une initiative destinée à servir l’intérêt général : « L’important de cette collaboration pour nous est d’œuvrer positivement pour la Guinée. Nous dirons que ce partenariat nous sera utile à l’UCEG et RMC dans l’intérêt commun de la Guinée », a-t-il indiqué. Dans le cadre de cet accord, RMC Cinéma prévoit notamment d’accompagner l’UCEG dans ses activités de sensibilisation à travers des sketches et d’autres productions cinématographiques. « En retour, nous nous engageons à les accompagner dans les sensibilisations, les sketches afin de faciliter la transmission des messages. Vu que nous sommes plus accessibles du point de vue communication, au lieu qu’ils effectuent de longs déplacements, nous nous engageons à faire passer leur message dans un temps bref à travers le cinéma », a-t-il expliqué. À travers ce partenariat, l’UCEG et RMC Cinéma 224 entendent donc conjuguer leurs expertises afin de faire de la création audiovisuelle un outil supplémentaire d’éducation citoyenne, de sensibilisation et de promotion des valeurs de paix et de cohésion sociale en Guinée. Mayi Cissé L’article Conakry : l’UCEG et RMC Cinéma officialisent un partenariat pour renforcer la sensibilisation citoyenne est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Algassimou Diallo transféré à Macenta : ses avocats demandent son retour à Conakry avant le 8 septembre
items.description: Le Collectif des avocats de l’ex-magistrat Algassimou DIALLO, poursuivi pour provocation à la discrimination, à la haine ou à la violence, discrimination et participation à une association de malfaiteurs, affirme avoir appris son transfèrement à la maison d’arrêt de Macenta par une publication de la Direction nationale de l’Administration pénitentiaire et de la Réinsertion diffusée sur les réseaux sociaux. Dans un communiqué publié dimanche 6 septembre 2026, la défense affirme n’avoir reçu aucune notification officielle concernant ce transfert intervenu le 5 septembre. Selon les avocats, ni la famille ni les conseils de Monsieur DIALLO n’avaient été informés de son nouveau lieu de détention. Le Collectif affirme avoir découvert cette information après avoir interrogé, la veille, les autorités judiciaires, qui auraient déclaré ne pas savoir où se trouvait l’ancien magistrat. Cette situation, selon la défense, ne suffit toutefois pas à dissiper les inquiétudes concernant « la vie, la sécurité et l’intégrité physique » de leur client. Les avocats indiquent que Monsieur DIALLO n’a été ni vu ni entendu depuis l’audience du 4 septembre, au cours de laquelle il était apparu, selon eux, « en bonne santé ». La défense souligne également que le transfèrement est intervenu au lendemain de cette audience, alors que les chambres réunies de la Cour suprême, siégeant à Conakry, doivent examiner le mardi 8 septembre la demande de renvoi formulée par les avocats. Elle relève que leur client se trouve désormais à plus de 700 kilomètres du siège de la juridiction devant laquelle il doit comparaître. Pour le Collectif, le motif de « gestion administrative des établissements pénitentiaires » invoqué pour justifier le transfert ne saurait, à lui seul, légitimer une telle mesure. Les avocats invoquent notamment les articles 1048, 1049 et 1050 du Code de procédure pénale, relatifs au lieu de détention provisoire, à l’exécution des ordres des magistrats et aux facilités devant être accordées aux personnes détenues pour l’exercice de leur défense. « Un inculpé détenu relève de l’autorité judiciaire, non de l’administration », soutient la défense. Face à ces préoccupations, les avocats demandent que la preuve de la détention d’Algassimou DIALLO à la maison d’arrêt de Macenta soit établie « sans délai », notamment par la production d’un extrait du registre d’écrou. Ils réclament également qu’une visite soit autorisée à sa famille et à ses conseils afin de leur permettre de vérifier son état. Le Collectif demande enfin que le fondement légal du transfèrement soit communiqué à la défense et que son client soit ramené à Conakry afin de pouvoir comparaître devant la Cour suprême le 8 septembre 2026. La Direction nationale de l’Administration pénitentiaire et de la Réinsertion avait annoncé le transfert d’Algassimou DIALLO à Macenta dans le cadre de la gestion administrative des établissements pénitentiaires. items.title: Septembre à Mbour (par Madou KANE)
items.description: Inscrit en lettres d’or dans l’agenda culturel de la ville, le ‘’Septembre mandingue’’ est organisé par la collectivité mandingue de Mbour. Chaque nouvelle édition part pour battre des records d’affluence. Une période idéale qui donne le tempo des vacances dans la cité côtière. Le Kankourang régne plus que jamais dans les coeurs des Mbourois, fait battre les pouls des Mandingues fiers de leur patrimoine. Dans ses multiples facettes, le mythe sacré se révèle. Discrètes et hautement mystiques, les sorties nocturnes du Kankourang, en semaine, intéressent les puristes, les ritualistes et les initiés de premier ordre. Des ‘’juju’’, dispersés dans les quartiers, s’échappent comme des complaintes, les chants mélancoliques des ‘’kasak’’ . Les tambours en sourdine accompagnent les petites voix des circoncis transis d’émotion. Parfois la mélodie et le rythme changent de ton, et de joyeux concerts égaillent ces soirées estivales. Un simple avant goût, en prélude de la grande messe du week-end en point de mire. La température monte dès vendredi quand affluent des myriades de visiteurs. Les Mbourois accueillent, dans leurs concessions, amis et voisins qu’ils ont côtoyés dans leurs univers scolaires ou professionnels. Les dames de la cité qui ont eu le toupet d’épouser des Sénégalais d’autres contrées désertent à l’amiable les maisons conjugales et retrouvent le bercail avec leurs progénitures. Autrement, impossible de les retenir, elles vous cherchent des noises et sont prêtes à mettre le divorce sur la table pour goûter aux délices carnavalesques du Kankourang. Les jeunes filles snobes et abonnées aux sulfureuses nuits dakaroises reprennent le visa pour la Petite Côte. Elles retrouvent un zeste d’originalité en regagnant, le temps des vacances, l’ambiance conviviale de familles qui ploient dans une promiscuité structurelle. La teranga qui opére dans la cité. Le fastueux dîner du samedi est offert aux visiteurs au grand dam des poulets victimes d’un sacrifice béni par le ‘’Kewoulo’’ au grand bonheur des gourmets. La veillée du samedi de septembre est sacrée. Les noctambules ignorent les chaudes boites de nuit et ingurgitent dans cette nuit blanche d’ambiance, du lait chaud à la menthe, concentré de fromage. Le ‘’mbourou’’, pain chaud et croustillant tartiné au beurre ou la ‘’balbina’’ de jadis, pain au lait, sucré et tendre, tiennent la dragée haute aux beignets et autres victuailles qui prolongent les retrouvailles dans la fraîcheur des terrasses ou aux devantures des maisons. Dans l’attente interminable, les connaisseurs guettent la sortie du Kankourang et prêtent l’oreille au tempo des tambours qui accompagnent les chants des initiés. Le protecteur des circoncis passera à l’aube après quelques fausses alertes qui ont semé de belles confusions et de mémorables frayeurs : les croustillantes anecdotes de la présente saison qui alimenteront longtemps les conversations à venir. Au soleil levant, le Kankourang s’exhibe enfin avec son bataillon d’initiés. Le fameux ‘’jaambo-jaambo’’ du petit matin est pour les puristes, le clou de la fête, le moment le plus exquis. Le tambour-major, comme inspiré par une muse, assène un rythme, venu d’ailleurs, qui déchaîne littéralement la foule qui a triomphé de la nuit pour ce moment de jouissance. Une belle occasion de danser, de chanter et de se défouler à satiété avant de retrouver les couchettes pour un sommeil lourd qui se prolonge en grâce matinée du dimanche. Au réveil, le ‘’mono’’ dominical, bouillie de mil version ‘’fondé’’ est servi dans les calebasses. Une bonne dose vous dope pour une journée qui sera forcément mouvementée. ‘’Mono’’ est aussi exquis que la viande du mouton de Tabaski ou le ‘’ngalakh’’ de Pâques. Que seraient devenus les Socés sans le ‘’mono’’ qui rassasie à moindre coût ? A quand la prochaine récolte de mil dans une ferme de la collectivité mandingue ? Dans l’après midi, à ‘’Bayal’’ Santessou, sur l’avenue Demba Diop ou à ‘’Kogne’’ Dialma, l’ambiance carnavalesque est indescriptible. Les nuées de spectateurs disséminées en ville prouvent la popularité presque démentielle d’un mythe incomparable. Les styles vestimentaires et les performances chorégraphiques comblent une foule en quête perpétuelle de loisirs. Madou KANE

items.title: Police in India's Gujarat publicly beat man accused of killing partner
items.description: Indian police publicly thrashed a man accused of beating his partner to death, local media reported on Sunday, drawing mixed reactions after footage of the flogging spread online. Public parading and beatings of suspects by police are not uncommon in India, despite Supreme Court rulings prohibiting such treatment. Officials said the thrashing was a response to the brutality of the alleged murder. The man, identified by police as Faizal Lakhani, was arrested in Bhavnagar, a town in Gujarat state. Police took Lakhani on Friday to the scene of the alleged crime to reconstruct the incident. He was beaten at the site, and footage of the battering was shared widely on social media. Videos show Lakhani’s arms restrained by ropes as a uniformed officer repeatedly struck his legs and buttocks with a bamboo baton. He was also beaten on his feet inside a bus terminal. “We beat him to set an example that crime against women will be taken seriously and nobody else dares to commit such a crime,” police officer DP Unadkat said, according to the Times of India newspaper. “When we do this, they fear the police,” Unadkat said, The Indian Express reported . Some social media users praised the beating while others denounced the police officers’ actions, with several X users saying the man had yet to be found guilty of the crime. Bhavnagar police chief Nitesh Pandey told AFP only: “I have nothing to comment.”

items.title: L’IACE plaide pour le développement du tourisme non conventionnel en Tunisie
items.description: L’Institut arabe des chefs d’entreprise (IACE) vient de publier sur son site web une étude intitulée «Évaluation économique & perspectives du tourisme non conventionnel en Tunisie» qui présente les opportunités, les défis et les leviers d’action pour faire émerger un tourisme tunisien plus diversifié, compétitif et durable. Le tourisme tunisien se trouve à un tournant. Après une décennie marquée par des crises successives et une reprise progressive, le secteur affiche de nouveau des performances solides : 7,5 milliards de dinars de recettes en 2024 et près de 8,2 milliards attendus en 2025, soit une progression d’environ 9%. Ces résultats confirment la capacité de résilience d’une filière stratégique pour l’économie nationale. Mais derrière cette embellie, le constat est clair : la Tunisie reste prisonnière d’un modèle centré sur le balnéaire, dépendant d’une forte saisonnalité et de quelques marchés européens. Or, le monde du tourisme change. Les voyageurs recherchent désormais plus d’authenticité, de bien-être, d’expériences personnalisées et responsables. Si la Tunisie veut rester compétitive dans l’espace méditerranéen face à l’Espagne, la Turquie ou le Maroc, elle doit accélérer sa diversification. C’est tout le sens de cette étude, première du genre en Tunisie à chiffrer le potentiel de cinq segments encore sous-exploités : tourisme senior, santé & bien-être, maisons d’hôtes et tourisme rural, haut de gamme, et locatif/plateformes. Les projections montrent qu’à l’horizon 2030, ces niches pourraient générer près de 2,7 milliards de dinars de recettes, soit près de 30% du total du secteur, et plus de 21500 emplois nouveaux. Autrement dit, la diversification n’est pas un supplément au modèle actuel : elle est la clé de son avenir. I. B. Lire l’étude intégrale. items.title: Bara Diouf, dix ans après, le souvenir d’une grande plume
items.description: Il y a dix ans, dans la nuit du 6 au 7 septembre 2016, le Sénégal perdait Bara Diouf, figure emblématique de la presse nationale. Décédé à l’âge de 89 ans, le journaliste aura marqué l’histoire des médias par son passage à l’Agence de presse sénégalaise (APS) et au quotidien Le Soleil, mais aussi par son rôle dans la formation de plusieurs générations de journalistes. Le 6 septembre reste une date de souvenir pour la presse nationale. Il y a dix ans, Bara Diouf disparaissait, laissant derrière lui une longue et riche carrière consacrée au journalisme, à la transmission et à la vie publique. La disparition de cette grande figure de la presse est intervenue dans la nuit du 6 au 7 septembre 2016, à Dakar. Cette précision explique que certaines sources retiennent le 6 septembre tandis que d’autres mentionnent le 7. Pour la mémoire collective, le 6 septembre demeure ainsi la date associée à l’hommage rendu au journaliste. Après des études à Paris, Bara Diouf avait commencé sa carrière au quotidien français Le Monde. De retour au Sénégal, il devient, en 1961, le premier Sénégalais à diriger l’Agence de presse sénégalaise, créée le 2 avril 1959. Il restera à la tête de l’APS jusqu’en 1964. En 1970, son parcours prend une nouvelle dimension avec la création du quotidien national Le Soleil, appelé à succéder au Dakar-Matin. Bara Diouf en devient le rédacteur en chef dès la naissance du journal, avant d’en assurer la direction de 1974 à 1988. Pionnier, grande plume et homme de transmission, il aura profondément marqué le journalisme sénégalais. À travers ses responsabilités et son expérience, il a contribué à former et à inspirer plusieurs générations de professionnels des médias. Une figure de la presse et de la vie politique L’histoire de Bara Diouf ne se limite toutefois pas au journalisme. Son parcours est également marqué par un engagement politique. Membre du Bureau politique de l’Union progressiste sénégalaise (UPS), puis du Parti socialiste, il poursuit cet engagement après son départ du Soleil, notamment comme député du Parti socialiste. Cette double trajectoire doit être replacée dans le contexte politique et médiatique du Sénégal de l’époque. À la création du Soleil, les liens entre le quotidien national et le parti au pouvoir étaient particulièrement étroits. Lors du congrès de l’UPS de 1969, Thierno Diop, alors secrétaire à la presse du parti, avait notamment exposé la conception que l’UPS se faisait du futur quotidien national. Le journal devait être lié au parti et son rédacteur en chef appelé à siéger au Bureau politique. La presse nationale était alors pensée comme un instrument d’animation, de vulgarisation, d’explication et de coordination, mais également comme un relais de la politique officielle. C’est dans ce contexte qu’il faut comprendre la double stature de Bara Diouf : celle d’un professionnel reconnu de la presse et celle d’un acteur engagé de la vie politique sénégalaise. Dix ans après, une mémoire toujours vivante Dix ans après sa disparition, le souvenir de Bara Diouf reste présent dans le monde de la presse. Ceux qui l’ont connu évoquent un journaliste exigeant, une grande plume et surtout un homme attaché à la transmission. Ce 6 septembre 2026, dix ans après sa disparition, Bara Diouf demeure ainsi une figure incontournable de l’histoire de la presse sénégalaise. Son nom reste associé à l’APS, au Soleil et à ces générations de journalistes auxquelles il a transmis une partie de son savoir et de son expérience. A.N

items.title: DirectAid concludes flood relief distribution across Greater Accra, Kasoa
items.description: Humanitarian organisation DirectAid Ghana has concluded the distribution of relief items to residents of communities affected by the June 2026 floods in Greater Accra and Kasoa in the Central Region. The exercise covered Alajo, Abofu-Achimota, Nana Krom-Lakeside-Santor, Abeka, Dansoman and Ablekuma-Manhea in the Greater Accra Region, as well as Kasoa in the Central Region. The intervention formed part of a wider relief programme by DirectAid to support families whose homes and livelihoods were affected by the floods. The programme was estimated at about GH¢2 million and was expected to benefit about 1,500 families. Beneficiaries received packages containing rice, litres of cooking oil, packs of spaghetti, beans, tomatoes and other food items. Household items, including mattresses, bedsheets, blankets, towels, soap and Parazone, were also distributed. The organisation said the relief items were provided with support from its donors in Kuwait, while government officials assisted in coordinating the exercise. DirectAid also indicated plans to extend assistance to clinics and hospitals with medical supplies and other items to support their operations. Call to stop activities that worsen flooding At the penultimate distribution in Dansoman, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of the Zongo Development Fund, Hajia Rakia Abdulai, urged residents to stop building on waterways and disposing of waste in drains. She said such practices contributed directly to flooding and called for more responsible lifestyles to help reduce the frequency and severity of flood disasters. While assuring affected persons of government support in times of disaster, Hajia Abdulai said preventive measures were equally important to protect lives and property. She expressed the hope that communities would increasingly come together to celebrate positive occasions rather than gather to sympathise with families who had suffered preventable losses of lives and property. The June floods affected several communities in Greater Accra and other parts of the country, leaving families with damaged homes and livelihoods. The relief exercise provided food and household essentials to affected families as they worked to recover from the disaster. The conclusion of the DirectAid exercise has renewed attention to the need for flood prevention measures alongside emergency relief, particularly enforcement against development on waterways and improved waste management. is

items.title: Volcano eruption leaves 150,000 passengers stranded in Indonesia
items.description: More than 150,000 passengers have been left stranded after a volcanic eruption forced Indonesian authorities to temporarily suspend operations at six airports. Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was the first to be closed on Sunday morning after ash from Anak Krakatau was detected in airspace near the airport. Transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi said so far 467 flights have been affected and asked airlines to consider diverting some flights to other airports. The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said. The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur. Purwagandhi said the decision to temporarily close more airports was made after tests found that volcanic ash had spread towards West Java. He urged airlines to speed up processes for refunding tickets for passengers who have been affected by flight cancellations, and for airlines to provide timely information to those with upcoming flights to avoid overcrowding at airports. According to Indonesia’s meteorological agency BMKG, ash reached as far as 20,000ft (6,000m) on Java on east of the volcano, and 50,000ft (15,000m) west of the volcano on the Sumatra side. Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra. The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks. According to local newspaper Kompas, several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents reported eye irritations from the ash, while some fishermen had cancelled fishing trips at sea similarly reporting sore eyes. One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told the outlet that he felt since Friday evening and it felt like “small grains of sand had gotten into my eyes”, and that he needs to use eye drops to ease the irritation. The dust is so thick that he has to sweep the front yard of his house every five minutes, he also said. Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa. The volcano – also known as Anak Krakatoa – collapsed in December 2018, triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java. Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high. The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand. Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that’s 452 individual active volcanoes.

items.title: Tunis accueille son 1er Forum international du halal
items.description: La Tunisie accueillera la première édition de l’International Halal Forum les 29 et 30 septembre 2026 au siège de la Maison de l’Exportateur, à Tunis, avec la participation des acteurs de l’écosystème halal aux niveaux national, régional et international. Organisé par le Global Business Network, sous l'égide du ministère du Commerce et du Développement des exportations et en coordination avec le Centre de promotion des exportations (Cepex), ce forum international réunira plusieurs institutions et organisations régionales et internationales œuvrant dans les domaines du halal, de la normalisation et du commerce, notamment l’Institut de normalisation et de métrologie pour les pays islamiques (Inpi, plus connu sous son acronyme anglais Smic), le Centre islamique pour le développement du commerce (CIDC) et l’Institut national de normalisation et de propriété industrielle (Innorpi). Selon les informations publiées par le Cepex, ce forum vise à explorer les moyens de développer les industries et les produits halal, à renforcer la coopération en matière de normalisation, de certification, de finance et de commerce, et à promouvoir les échanges économiques et les partenariats entre les acteurs de ce secteur en Afrique, dans les pays du Golfe, en Asie et en Europe. Le programme du forum comprend des séances plénières, des tables rondes spécialisées et des ateliers techniques, ainsi que des rencontres interentreprises. L’objectif est de faciliter la mise en réseau des participants et d’explorer les opportunités de collaboration, d’investissement et de création de partenariats économiques et commerciaux. Le forum disposera également d’un espace d’exposition présentant des produits, des solutions et des initiatives halal susceptibles d’accéder aux marchés internationaux, permettant ainsi aux entreprises participantes de mettre en valeur leurs atouts et de nouer des contacts avec des partenaires potentiels. Le forum devrait réunir des représentants d’institutions gouvernementales, d’organismes de normalisation et de certification halal, ainsi que des représentants d’institutions financières, des dirigeants d’organisations économiques, des investisseurs stratégiques et des représentants de divers acteurs de l’écosystème halal aux niveaux régional et international. items.title: Le Président de la République appelle à imprimer un cachet populaire aux JOJ Dakar 2026
items.description: Le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye exhorte le peuple Sénégalais à faire des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026 une cause nationale et un projet collectif. Il appelle à cet égard, à une forte mobilisation afin que cet événement enregistre pleinement l'implication de l’ensemble des couches de la société. À l’approche des Jeux Olympiques de la Jeunesse, les autorités sénégalaises, en plus d’insister sur le défi organisationnel montrent la voie sur l’incontournable nécessité d’imprimer à cet événement international, un cachet populaire, voire même fédérateur. Il est prévu, entre autres, la distribution de 150 000 kits scolaires aux élèves et aux enseignants, afin de les sensibiliser à la portée historique de l’organisation des JOJ par le Sénégal, premier pays africain à accueillir cette compétition. Ces supports vont faciliter aux enseignants à expliquer aux élèves l’honneur qu’englobe la confiance de la communauté internationale, à travers l’organisation de cet événement inédit sur le continent. 200 000 billets seront mis à la disposition des écoles et des associations, pour permettre aux enfants toutes couches sociales confondues, sans discrimination, d’assister aux différentes compétitions. Par ailleurs, la Fondation Sénégal Solidaire, contribuera à hauteur de 500 millions de francs CFA à la mobilisation autour des Jeux, annonce le chef de l’Etat. Un grand événement sportif ne se mesure pas uniquement à la qualité des infrastructures ou au respect du cahier des charges. Il se mesure aussi à sa capacité à fédérer une population, à créer un imaginaire collectif et à laisser une empreinte dans la mémoire nationale. C’est précisément là que se situe l’un des principaux défis des JOJ. Le président de la République l’a si bien compris au point qu’il s’implique personnellement. Dans la journée du samedi 5 septembre, il s’est déplacé pour lancer la campagne d’embellissement et de végétalisation des alentours du stade Léopold Sédar Senghor. Le soir même, il a présidé le lancement officiel de « Dundal JOJ ». Un programme qui a pour but d’imprimer un cachet national aux jeux, en les projetant dans toutes les localités du pays. Le lancement a réuni : entrepreneurs, hommes d’affaires, diplomates, artistes, membres du gouvernement et acteurs sportifs. A travers cette approche, le chef de l’Etat lance un message on ne peut plus implicite « les JOJ ne doivent pas être perçus comme une affaire réservée aux athlètes, aux responsables sportifs, aux institutions et aux délégations étrangères. Ils doivent devenir les Jeux des jeunes, des quartiers, des écoles, des familles et des territoires ». Cela suppose une véritable stratégie de mobilisation populaire : animations dans les quartiers, manifestations culturelles, concerts, activités sportives, initiatives citoyennes et implication des collectivités locales. L’objectif n’est pas de transformer les JOJ en simple festival. items.title: Six Movies to Get You in the Fall Mood
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. September has arrived, bringing the first hints of fall: cooler days, changing leaves, and the urge to revisit comfort watches. Below, The Atlantic ’s writers and editors recommend six films that put them in an autumn spirit. When Harry Met Sally (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV) There’s the cornucopia of cable-knit sweaters, a chocolate-brown velvet bowler hat, the fog of bright-orange leaves streaming through the glass wall at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Autumn in New York is the backdrop of When Harry Met Sally , but that doesn’t fully account for the place that Nora Ephron and Rob Reiner’s classic occupies in my life: For me, it’s the chicken noodle soup of movies. I have my personal reasons for considering it the ultimate comfort watch. Maybe it’s my affinity with Sally (played by Meg Ryan), the curly-haired journalist determined to have life happen to her, though her job is to “write about things that happen to other people.” Or the movie’s love for my hometown, which forms the bedrock of so many of Ephron’s films. Or the weirdly specific fantasy of having your date unwittingly quote to you something you wrote in a magazine . This time of year, I’m far from the only person who considers a When Harry Met Sally rewatch as inevitable as digging my denim jacket out of the back of my closet. If there’s a universal magic to the movie, maybe some of it comes from magic in real life. The original script saw Sally and Harry’s (Billy Crystal) story ending bittersweetly, with the two apart. But midway through making the film, Reiner fell in love with his wife, Michele Singer. This fall—our first without Reiner and Singer —I’ll be revisiting the movie in large part for the ending he decided on instead: perhaps the most memorable, and certainly my favorite, in the romantic-comedy genre. — Marie-Rose Sheinerman, assistant editor *** Michael Clayton (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV) Fall is not really about melancholy and the inner life, as the poets would have you believe. It’s that period, after summer’s frivolities, when things get serious again. Michael Clayton , a film I first saw at the urging of my friend and colleague James Parker—and which we both regularly rewatch—is charged with that urban, autumnal, overcoated feeling of things getting serious. The people in it are grown-ups. If they’re not, as with Timmy—Michael Clayton’s brother, whose feckless behavior leaves Michael exposed to loan sharks—they’re basically ignored. Sydney Pollack? What a performance! What an impeccably serious guy! Tom Wilkinson, Tilda Swinton—they’re brilliant in this. And George Clooney, playing the titular character, is haunted by his own rotting, inky-eyed charm and stymied at every turn, despite his good intentions. He’s at his best in the scene where Michael, working as his law firm’s fixer, advises an affluent, arrogant client who has just committed a hit-and-run. The client, thinking it’s still unfettered summer, throws a childish tantrum. Michael, in his best autumnal mode, sets him straight: “There’s no play here. There’s no angle. There’s no champagne room. And I’m not a miracle worker; I’m a janitor.” — Sebastian Smee, staff writer *** Little Women (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV) Fall is a happy-sad season: The sunlight is golden (but that’s a sign that the days are getting shorter), the leaves are ochre and maroon (a sign that they’re dying), and the air is crisp (a sign of impending winter). And to me, Greta Gerwig’s 2019 adaptation of Little Women perfectly embodies this feeling. The story follows the four March sisters through the different seasons of their life. Their childhood flashbacks are scenes captured in warm, autumnal tones, and adulthood flash-forwards are shot in cooler, harsher light, to reflect the girls’ feelings about the passage of time. Jo March wants to grow up, and yet she clings to girlhood, panicking as those around her—such as her sister Meg, who gets married—seem content to let the past go. In one pivotal scene, Jo tells her mother that she wishes she could still want what she wanted as a child, when simply being with her family was enough. Now her aspirations for a career and romantic love seem at odds, and her sense of independence has become inextricable from an acute sense of loneliness. For those of us who also cling to the past (even if that past is just “summer”), this film will comfort you and remind you that change is inevitable. — Nancy Walecki, staff writer *** You’ve Got Mail (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV) The first 30 minutes of You’ve Got Mail are an unabashed ode to autumn. “Don’t you love New York in the fall?” the film’s romantic hero, Joe (Tom Hanks), writes in an email to the heroine, Kathleen (Meg Ryan). When Kathleen arrives at work a few minutes later with a perfect orange pumpkin under her arm, she breathlessly repeats the question: “Don’t you just love New York in the fall?” And how could you not? The film shows children bobbing for apples at a street fair, a tree with copper leaves set against a row of brownstones, and characters walking around the Upper West Side in good knits, blazers, and fleeces. Even when the movie shifts to winter and then spring, You’ve Got Mail still feels autumnal. That feeling goes beyond the scenery: It’s a wistful movie, and at times a sad one. Characters major and minor express regret over lost loves, broken family relationships, and unrealized dreams. Kathleen and Joe spend most of the film in relationships with people they clearly do not love. These notes of melancholy make it a perfect romantic comedy to turn to as the days get shorter. — Eleanor Barkhorn, senior editor *** Point Break (streaming on Peacock) I grew up in Los Angeles, and as a result, I do not really understand seasons, weather, or people’s fear of being seen perspiring. Since I moved to the East Coast eight years ago, I have found autumn to be a cute but unwelcome reminder that winter is real and, even worse, that I will soon be forced to experience it. The 1991 action thriller Point Break is also about Angeleno men who do not condone the end of summer. In the movie, they take this aversion one step further, robbing banks to fund the travel necessary to never stop surfing under the hot sun. The dialogue is clunky, albeit quotable, and almost nothing about the plot is believable. And yet, it’s so fun to watch these guys, and the FBI agent who tails them, try to make one summer weekend last forever. That is how I will be spending the fall: in denial, doing as much hiking, paddleboarding, and swimming as possible, until I am forced to stop. — Marc Novicoff, staff writer *** Silent Friend (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV) Silent Friend is a meandering film that has nudged me toward accepting slowness and inevitable change. The historical drama follows three environmentalists at a German university across three epochs as each tries to uncover the secret life of plants: In 1908, Grete navigates sexism and her own position as one of the first female students in the university’s botany department; in 1972, a young man named Hannes, immersed in his college campus’s Cold War–era counterculture, develops sensors to understand how a potted geranium perceives him; and in 2020, a neuroscientist runs an experiment connecting a tree’s electrical activity with his own after the COVID lockdown cuts off his access to human subjects. At the center of it all is a nearly 200-year-old ginkgo tree that provides quiet solace to the three characters. The tree becomes a central figure in the story, observing, listening, and breathing alongside its subjects. Its presence embodies the spirit of the film, which is more sensory-driven than narrative-driven and makes it easy to lose yourself in the foliage. Now every time I see a leaf change color, I’m reminded to pay closer attention to the natural world around me and all of the life that brims within it. — Kim Jao, assistant editor Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : Inside a conservative operation to hijack your social-media feed The White House wants to make the Smithsonian a pariah. The growing lawlessness in California’s forests The Week Ahead The Uprising , a drama-action film based on the true story that’s said to have inspired the legend of Robin Hood (in theaters Friday) The Art of Fighting , a book by Priya Parker on the power of conflict (out Tuesday) Last Seen , a thriller series about a police dispatcher who receives a call from a teenager he believes could be his daughter, who disappeared 11 years earlier (streaming Wednesday on Apple TV) Essay Branden Eastwood / AFP / Getty The Measles-Stricken Mother Who Lost Her Newborn Son By Tom Bartlett When the Amish man emerged from his barn to greet me, he had no idea that his newborn son’s death had become national news. The man wore a straw hat, black trousers, and suspenders over a long-sleeved blue shirt; one of his similarly dressed sons was guiding a horse-drawn plow in a nearby field. The man told me that, like most Amish people, he and his family don’t watch TV or use the internet. They don’t read the newspaper either. So they didn’t know until I told them that last Tuesday, Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, held a press conference to announce the first two “measles-associated” deaths in the state in 35 years.
